definition: The empirical curves relating accuracy to test-time compute, whether spent in parallel (more samples plus selection) or sequentially (longer chains), and the finding that a small model with search can rival a larger model without it.
details: The empirical curves relating accuracy to test-time compute, whether spent in parallel (more samples plus selection) or sequentially (longer chains), and the finding that a small model with search can rival a larger model without it. The economic logic behind the shift from pure pretraining scale to reasoning-time scale.

explainer.lead: These laws describe how accuracy rises with test-time compute, whether spent in parallel (more samples plus selection) or sequentially (longer chains). They are the economic logic behind shifting from pure pretraining scale to reasoning-time scale.

tiers.eli5: Sometimes letting a model think longer, or try several answers and pick the best, works nearly as well as using a bigger model.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers trade model size against compute at inference: more samples or longer chains can close the gap to a larger model. The pitfall is that returns diminish, so extra compute eventually buys little accuracy.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, empirical curves relate accuracy to test-time compute, parallel (more samples plus selection) or sequential (longer chains). A known finding is that a small model with search can rival a larger model without it.

explainer.example: A small model that generates many candidate answers and selects among them can match a larger model's accuracy on a reasoning task.
